questions.enonce_markdown:
Distinguish between an Incorporated and an Unincorporated business using suitable examples.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Businesses are classified according to whether the law treats them as separate from their owners. This gives incorporated and unincorporated businesses.

| | Incorporated business | Unincorporated business |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | A business that has been **registered as a company** and has its own legal personality, separate from its owners. | A business that has **no legal personality separate from its owner(s)**; the owner and the business are one in law. |
| Legal identity | It can own property, sign contracts, sue and be sued **in its own name**. | The owner(s) own the property and sign contracts, and are sued personally. |
| Liability of owners | Usually **limited**: shareholders lose only the money they invested. | Usually **unlimited**: the owner's private property can be used to pay the business debts. |
| Continuity | **Perpetual succession**: the business continues when a shareholder dies or leaves. | It may end with the death, bankruptcy or withdrawal of the owner or of a partner. |
| Formation | Needs formal registration and documents (for example a memorandum and articles of association). | Easy and cheap to start; few legal formalities. |
| Capital | Can raise large capital by selling shares. | Capital is limited to the savings and loans of the owner(s). |
| Examples | A private limited company, a public limited company. | A sole trader (a boutique owner or a roadside trader in Douala), an ordinary partnership of two tailors. |

**Conclusion.** An incorporated business is a separate legal person with limited liability, while an unincorporated business is legally the same as its owner(s).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain any FOUR advantages of a sole trader as a form of business.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A sole trader is a business owned, financed and usually run by one person, such as the owner of a small provision shop. Its main advantages are the following.

1. **Easy and cheap to set up.** Few legal formalities are needed and little capital is required, so a person with modest savings can start trading quickly.
2. **Full control and quick decisions.** The owner takes every decision alone, without consulting partners or shareholders, so he can react quickly to changes in customers' demand.
3. **The owner keeps all the profit.** No profit is shared with partners or shareholders, which motivates the owner to work hard.
4. **Personal contact with customers.** The owner knows his customers, their tastes and their needs, which builds loyalty and good service.
5. **Secrecy.** The owner does not have to publish accounts, so competitors cannot easily learn about his business.
6. **Flexibility.** He can choose his own opening hours and change the goods he sells without permission from anyone.

(Any four of these, each explained, earn full marks.)

**Conclusion.** The sole trader form is simple, flexible and rewarding for small businesses.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Outline any SIX features of co-operative societies.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A co-operative society is an organisation of people who join voluntarily to meet their common economic needs by working together. Its main features are:

1. **Voluntary membership.** Anybody who meets the conditions may join or leave freely.
2. **Common interest.** Members share a need, for example farmers who want to sell their cocoa or coffee together or workers who want cheap credit.
3. **Democratic control.** Each member has **one vote**, whatever the number of shares he holds ("one man, one vote").
4. **Capital from members.** The capital is raised from members' shares and savings, and each member usually has a limited number of shares.
5. **Limited liability.** In most co-operatives members are liable only for the value of their shares.
6. **Separate legal identity.** A registered society can own property and sign contracts in its own name.
7. **Service before profit.** The aim is to serve members, for example by giving better prices, loans or cheaper goods.
8. **Surplus shared among members.** The surplus is shared according to the trade each member did with the society (dividend or bonus on purchases or sales) and not only according to shares, and part is kept as a reserve.
9. **Management by an elected committee.** Members elect a management committee which runs the society for them.

(Any six of these features earn full marks.)
